transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. Um, it's a bit of a long story, I suppose, but what finally made me agree to actually come in and sit down with someone is that... well, I just don't care about the things that used to keep me balanced. 

I'm a project management specialist, so my whole life is usually about structure and balancing the stress of work with proper downtime, you know? But lately, I just... I can't be bothered. Like the sailing races, for instance. I used to live for those. I'd be checking the weather on Tuesday, prepping the rigging by Thursday, getting the crew all coordinated... and now I haven't even been down to the marina in I don't know how long. 

And it's not just the big things like sailing. I have this Saturday shift at the local historical society—I've done it for years, sorting through old township records, which sounds incredibly tedious to most people, I know, but I always really loved it. Now, I just keep calling out. Even just going out to the garage and tinkering in the woodshop... I've got a half-finished cherry wood table out there that's just gathering dust because I can't bring myself to pick up a sander. 

All of it, everything that used to be my escape, it all just feels like... like these massive chores that I keep putting off. I just have zero interest in any of it anymore, and it's starting to feel like a real problem.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time lately?

Sad? No, I... I wouldn't use that word. It's funny you ask that, actually, because my brother-in-law was asking me something very similar just the other week. We were supposed to go to this regional hardware expo together—he's an independent contractor, and I usually tag along just to look at new tools for the woodshop I mentioned earlier—and when I called to tell him I wasn't going to make it, he got all quiet and asked if I was depressed or feeling down. 

And I had to explain to him, and I guess I should explain it to you too, that it's really not a sadness. I'm not sitting around weeping or, you know, feeling miserable or sorry for myself. I don't have this heavy, dark cloud of sorrow following me around everywhere. It's more just... well, it's a blankness. 

Like, in my line of work, if a project you're managing is actively failing, you feel stressed, you feel upset, you have an emotional reaction to it. But if a project is just canceled entirely, you just pack up the files, put them in a drawer, and you feel nothing. That's kind of where I'm at. I get up in the morning, I make my coffee—I've got this whole pour-over setup that usually takes a good ten minutes to do right, measuring the water temperature, blooming the grounds and everything—and I just drink it and feel completely neutral. There's no emotional low, but there's just no high either. I'm just going through the mechanical motions. So, no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad most of the time. I'm not really feeling much of anything at all.
How long have you been feeling this way, with no interest in your usual activities and feeling neutral most of the time?

Well, let me think about the exact timeline. It's funny how time sort of blurs together when you're just going through the motions, you know? But I can pinpoint it pretty exactly, actually. It's been a little over a year now. 

It all started right around the time of this massive business readjustment we were going through at work. As a project management specialist, those periods are always incredibly intense—we were restructuring three different departments, reallocating resources, dealing with new vendors, the whole nine yards. I was working long hours, which I'm used to, but there was this specific incident right in the middle of it all. There was a scaffold accident on one of our active sites. 

I won't get into all the technical details of the site management, but it was a major disruption, obviously. And it's really since that exact period—since that accident during the readjustment—that this whole... blankness, this total lack of interest in the sailing and the woodshop and everything else, really set in. So, yeah, I'd say it's been a little over a year that I've been stuck in this sort of neutral gear. I kept thinking it would pass once the readjustment was finalized and the dust settled from the accident, but it just... hasn't. The calendar keeps turning, but I'm still just feeling exactly the same way.
Have you noticed any decrease in pleasure when you do engage in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, actually. That's exactly it. When I do manage to force myself to do something, or even just in my day-to-day life, there's just... nothing there. The reward is gone. 

Like, take my family, for instance. I've been married for twenty-two years, we have three kids, and we've always had these big, loud, chaotic family dinners. Especially on Sundays. My wife makes this incredible roast, and the kids are all talking over each other, telling jokes, arguing about some movie they saw... and usually, that's the highlight of my week. I love that noise. I love seeing them happy. But lately... well, for the past year, really... I sit at the head of the table, and they can all be laughing until they're practically in tears over something my youngest said, and I just... I know I should feel good. I know I should be smiling and laughing right along with them, feeling that warmth you're supposed to feel when your family is happy. But mostly, I just feel flat. I feel completely removed from it, like I'm watching them through a pane of thick glass. 

And it's the same at work, too. As a project management specialist, a huge part of the job is hitting those major milestones. You know, when you finally get the sign-off from the city planners, or when the framing is officially completed ahead of schedule and under budget. Those moments used to give me a real rush, a real sense of accomplishment and pride. I'd take the team out for drinks, or at least feel a solid pat on my own back. But now? I can finish a incredibly difficult, complex project milestone—something that took weeks of coordination and putting out fires—and when I check that box, I don't feel a thing. No relief, no pride, no joy. Just... flat. It's like the part of my brain that registers a good feeling has just been unplugged. So, yes, even when I am doing things that should make me happy, or that used to bring me pleasure, that feeling is just entirely absent.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past year?

Weight? No, no, my weight has been pretty much exactly the same. I haven't noticed any significant change at all, really. 

It's actually kind of surprising, considering everything else. You know, I've always been one of those guys whose weight fluctuates depending on how busy I am. Like, back when I was managing the downtown revitalization project—this was maybe six or seven years ago, a massive undertaking with city council breathing down my neck every single day—I dropped maybe ten pounds just from running around the site and forgetting to eat lunch. And then, conversely, during the slow winter months, I usually put on a few pounds because I'm stuck at a desk doing paperwork and eating those terrible pastries they bring into the breakroom. 

But over this past year? Nothing. I step on the scale in the morning—it's this digital one my wife bought, tracks your BMI and bone density and all that, though I don't really pay attention to those numbers—and the number is just stubbornly consistent. I'm right around 185, which is where I've been for a while. 

And my appetite hasn't really changed either, which I suppose is why the weight hasn't changed. I still eat exactly what I usually eat. I still have my pour-over coffee and a piece of toast in the morning, I still eat whatever sandwich or salad I pack for lunch, and I still eat the dinners my wife makes. The difference is just that I don't really care about the food anymore. Like that Sunday roast I mentioned earlier? It used to be my favorite meal. Now, I eat it, and I know intellectually that it's cooked well, but it just tastes like... fuel. I'm just chewing and swallowing because it's dinnertime and that's what you do. There's no enjoyment in it. But I'm still eating the same portions, still keeping the same routine, so the weight has stayed exactly the same. So, no, no weight loss or gain to speak of. Just staying right where I am.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or lacking energy lately?

Energy? No, not really. I mean, I'm not bouncing off the walls, obviously, but I wouldn't say I'm unusually tired or lacking energy, no. 

It's actually kind of a strange feeling, to be honest. You'd think with this whole... flat feeling, this lack of interest in everything, that I'd just want to stay in bed all day. I know that's how it goes for some people. My sister-in-law went through a rough patch a few years ago, and she could barely get off the couch. But for me, it's not like that. I still get up at 5:30 every morning, just like I have for the last twenty years. I go through the motions. I shower, I get dressed, I make my coffee, I commute to the office or the site, whichever I'm assigned to that day. I do the work. I have the physical stamina to get through the day, same as always. 

Like yesterday, for example. We had a massive concrete pour scheduled for a new commercial build downtown. Those days are grueling. You're on your feet for hours, coordinating with the foremen, making sure the trucks are arriving on schedule, checking the slump... it's a lot of physical and mental exertion. And I did it. I was out there in the hard hat and boots, walking the site, climbing up and down the temporary stairs, talking to everyone. I didn't feel physically exhausted or like I needed to sit down or take a nap. My body was doing exactly what it's supposed to do. I had the energy to complete the tasks. 

The problem isn't the energy itself, it's the... the drive behind it, I guess. I have the physical battery power to do the work, but there's no spark. I'm just operating like a machine. A machine that's fully charged but doesn't really care what it's building. So, physically, I'm not unusually tired. I'm not dragging myself around or needing extra sleep. I still get my seven hours a night and wake up when the alarm goes off. It's just that when I wake up, I'm not looking forward to using that energy for anything. But the energy itself? No, that hasn't changed. I'm still functioning at my normal capacity, physically speaking.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear?

Thoughts of not wanting to be alive? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I know I just spent all that time explaining how flat everything feels, and how I'm just sort of operating like a machine that doesn't care about what it's building, but... it hasn't gone to that extreme. Not at all. 

I don't want to die, and I don't want to disappear. It's more like... well, like I said, I'm just present but unplugged. But I *am* present. I have to be. I mean, think about my family, right? My wife and the three kids. My oldest is actually just finishing up her bachelor's degree—she's studying architecture, which I like to think she got a little bit of inspiration from my line of work, though she'd probably completely deny it if you asked her—and my youngest is still navigating high school. I couldn't just... check out on them. I'm their father. I provide for them. Even if I'm sitting at that Sunday dinner table feeling completely detached from the laughter and the noise, I still know, intellectually, that my place is at the head of that table. 

And it's the same with my job. As a project management specialist, you are the linchpin of the whole operation. If I were to just disappear, the cascading effect on the scheduling, the budget, the sub-contractors... it would be an absolute nightmare for the firm. I've got a crew of eighty guys on this current commercial build downtown who rely on me to make sure the materials are there on time so they can get their hours in and feed their own families. 

So, no, the sense of duty is still very much intact, even if the joy isn't. I don't have any desire to end things or vanish. I just... I just wish I could feel like myself while I'm doing all of it, you know? But as far as wanting to not be alive, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that whatsoever. I'm firmly planted right here, for better or worse.
Do you often feel guilty or reproach yourself for things that have happened?

Guilty? Yeah... yeah, actually, I do. It's funny you use that word, because... well, in my line of work, as a project manager, your whole job is basically foreseeing the unforeseen, right? You build out these massive risk assessment matrices. You sit in these endless meetings calculating the probability of supply chain delays, weather events, labor shortages, equipment failures, you name it. You have contingency plans for your contingency plans. You're supposed to be the guy who sees around corners.

So lately, there's just this... this constant, low-grade dread and guilt that follows me around everywhere I go. It's like a shadow. I wake up with it, I take it to the job site, I bring it home to the dinner table. It's this nagging, heavy feeling like I should have seen one more risk coming. Like if I had just looked at the variables a little differently, or pushed a little harder during a site inspection, or anticipated that one tiny flaw in the system, things would be different. I just keep running through the sequence of events in my head, over and over, looking for the exact moment I should have intervened.

And the logical part of my brain—and frankly, everyone around me—keeps telling me otherwise. My colleagues, the higher-ups at the firm, they all keep telling me that the controls were in place. They pull out the documentation and say, "Look, you followed the protocols to the letter, you couldn't have known, the safety measures were completely standard for a build this size." And I hear them saying the words. I know they mean well, and I know on paper, technically, they're right. The compliance checks were all signed off. 

But it doesn't change this... this pit in my stomach. It just sits there, this guilt, making me rehash every decision, every memo, every walk-through, wondering what I missed. Because someone in my position is supposed to catch everything, you know? That's literally what they pay me for, to mitigate risk. So even when everyone else absolves me and tells me the controls were functioning as designed, I just can't seem to shake this awful, pervasive dread that I failed to see the one risk that actually mattered. It's exhausting, honestly, just carrying that around all day.
Have you noticed yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Moving more slowly? Reacting slower? No, no, I haven't noticed anything like that. Physically, my reaction times are just as sharp as they've always been. I mean, you really have to be quick on your feet on a commercial build site. Just the other day, for instance, we were coordinating a massive delivery of steel I-beams, and you've got cranes operating overhead, you've got skid steers and forklifts zipping around, and eighty guys trying to get their jobs done in a very confined footprint. If you're moving slowly out there, or if your reflexes are delayed, you're a massive liability. You could get yourself seriously injured, or worse, cause an accident that hurts someone else. So no, my physical reactions are completely fine. I'm still dodging out of the way of machinery, climbing up scaffolding, navigating the uneven terrain of the foundation pours without missing a beat. I can catch a falling clipboard before it hits the dirt, you know? 

Like I was saying earlier when we were talking about my energy levels, the physical machinery of my body is working perfectly fine. I drive my truck on the highway every day, my reflexes are sharp, I brake when I need to brake, I merge just fine. It's definitely not a physical slowness. If anything, sometimes I feel like I'm almost rushing through the physical motions just to get the day over with, just putting one foot in front of the other at a completely normal, or even a brisk pace. My wife actually pointed out just this past weekend that I walk way too fast when we go to the hardware store or the grocery store. She's always telling me to slow down and wait for her in the aisles. 

So, yeah, physically, my reaction time hasn't taken a hit at all. It's just that mental weight I'm carrying, that heavy dread and the guilt I was just telling you about. It feels heavy in my mind, but it doesn't actually translate to my limbs or my walking speed or my physical reflexes. Those are all completely intact. I mean, I'm fifty-one, so obviously I'm not sprinting around like a high school track star anymore, but compared to my normal baseline over the last few years? No change whatsoever. I'm still moving and reacting at my regular, normal speed. No sluggishness there at all.
Do you find yourself fidgeting or restless, or do you feel like you're stuck in place and can't seem to get moving?

Stuck in place? No, no, definitely not. Like I was just saying a minute ago about my reaction times and how I move around the site, I don't have any trouble getting moving. When the alarm goes off at 4:30 AM, I'm up, my feet hit the floor, and I'm moving. I don't just lie there frozen or feeling like my limbs are filled with lead or anything like that. I get right to the coffee maker, get my boots on, and head out the door to the site. So being stuck is definitely not an issue for me. 

And as for being restless or fidgeting... no, I wouldn't say I do that either. I mean, I spend half my week out on the dirt, but the other half is just sitting in these incredibly long, drawn-out alignment meetings. You know, you get the architects, the structural engineers, the city inspectors, and the client reps all crammed into one temporary trailer or a rented conference room, and you're just hashing out budget variances and schedule adjustments for three hours straight. And I sit through all of that completely still. I'm not bouncing my leg under the table, I'm not clicking my pen a hundred times a minute, I don't have to keep getting up to pace around the room or get a drink of water just to burn off energy. 

It's actually kind of strange when you think about it, because, like I was telling you earlier, I've got this constant, heavy dread and guilt just sitting in my stomach all the time, making me rethink every single decision and protocol. You'd think that kind of internal noise would make a guy jumpy or restless, right? You'd think I'd be pacing holes in the floorboards at home. But I don't. I just sit there in my recliner in the living room in the evenings while my wife watches her shows, or I sit at the head of the conference table at work, and I'm completely, totally still. Physically, anyway. 

My mind is obviously running a mile a minute trying to figure out what I missed and rehashing the risk matrices, but my body... my body is just doing exactly what it's supposed to do. Not stuck, not restless, just... normal. I'm not agitated. I just get up, do the job, sit when I need to sit, and walk when I need to walk. So, yeah, neither of those things really apply to me.
Have you been having trouble concentrating on things lately?

Trouble concentrating? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Actually, my focus is probably one of the only things working exactly the way it's supposed to right now. I mean, you have to understand, in project management—especially on the scale of the commercial builds I oversee—if you lose your concentration for even five minutes while you're reviewing a contract or a structural schematic, you can cost the client hundreds of thousands of dollars. Or worse, you compromise the integrity of the build. 

Just to give you an example, on Tuesday, I had to sit down and review this massive, 400-page revision to an electrical plan because the city decided to update their compliance codes right in the middle of our Q3 timeline. I sat at my desk in the trailer, locked in, for maybe four and a half hours straight, just cross-referencing the new conduit requirements against our existing supply orders. Didn't miss a beat. I didn't find myself zoning out, I didn't have to re-read the same paragraph over and over to understand it. I actually caught three minor discrepancies that the engineering firm themselves missed. 

So, my ability to just zero in on a task, to really concentrate on the fine print, is completely intact. It's almost like... well, like I was telling you earlier about that dread and that guilt I have about missing a risk? Because I have that hanging over me all the time, I feel like I'm almost hyper-focused when I'm looking at documents or schedules now. I'm staring at these spreadsheets and blueprints with a magnifying glass because I absolutely refuse to let a single variable slip by me. 

And it's the same at home, too. I can sit down and read a biography, or help my nephew with his calculus homework when he comes over, or balance our personal finances without my mind wandering off into the clouds. The concentration is definitely there. It's just... the things my mind chooses to focus on when I'm *not* actively working on a task, you know? That's when it goes right back to rehashing the past and looking for where I failed. But when I need to apply myself to something right in front of me, whether it's a site inspection report or just following the complicated plot of some British mystery show with my wife, I can lock right in. No issues with my concentration whatsoever.
Do you often feel worthless or that you're a burden to others?

Worthless? A burden? No... no, I wouldn't say that. Not at all. I mean, I can see why you might ask that, given the heavy guilt I was talking about earlier, feeling like I missed things or didn't do enough to foresee a risk. But there's a very big difference, at least in my mind, between feeling guilty about a specific protocol and feeling completely worthless as a person. 

I know my value. I've been in commercial project management for over twenty years now, and you just don't survive in this industry—managing multi-million dollar budgets, coordinating eighty different subcontractors on a tight footprint—if you're worthless. I know I'm good at what I do. I provide a very comfortable life for my wife. We actually managed to pay off our mortgage three years early, which is something I take a whole lot of pride in. 

And as for being a burden... no, if anything, I'm the one carrying the load for other people. I'm the guy everyone calls when things go sideways. Just to give you an idea, last weekend, my brother-in-law's sump pump failed in his basement. Who does he call at eleven o'clock on a Saturday night? Me. Because he knows I've got the heavy-duty wet-vac in the garage, I have the industrial fans, and I know exactly how to pull up the baseboards without completely ruining the drywall. I drove over there in the pouring rain and spent four hours bailing him out. Literally bailing him out. 

So, I'm definitely not a burden. People rely on me. My crew relies on me to keep the site safe and make sure the supply chains are moving so their paychecks clear, my wife relies on me, my extended family relies on me. Even with this dread hanging over me, this constant, exhausting mental loop of re-checking my decisions to make sure nobody gets hurt... I know I'm useful. I know I have a purpose. I'm a provider and a problem-solver, and that fundamental part of who I am hasn't changed one bit. I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking the world would be better off without me, or anything dramatic like that. I just want to figure out how to shut off the internal noise. But my actual self-worth? No, that's completely intact.
Do you find yourself pacing back and forth or feeling an intense need to be in constant motion when you're not working?

Well, I think that kind of goes back to what we were talking about a few minutes ago with the restlessness, so... no, definitely not. When I'm not working, when I finally get off the clock and get home after a twelve-hour day managing the site, I really just stop. My body just stops. I don't have this urge to get up and walk laps around the kitchen island or anything like that. 

Take last Sunday, for example. We didn't have any family obligations, the whole sump pump disaster with my brother-in-law from the previous weekend was already handled, and my wife was out back doing some planting in her garden beds. I came inside, grabbed a glass of ice water, and sat down in my leather recliner in the den. It's one of those oversized ones, you know, the kind with the heavy-duty lumbar support? I have to have that because my lower back gets pretty tight from walking on uneven dirt and concrete in steel-toe boots all week. Anyway, I sat down in that chair, turned on a documentary about the engineering of the Panama Canal—which is fascinating, by the way, the sheer scale of the earth-moving they had to do back then with such limited technology—and I just sat there. For probably three, maybe three and a half solid hours. Completely still. 

I wasn't pacing the hallways, I wasn't feeling like I needed to go organize the garage or burn off some kind of nervous physical energy. I wasn't even really watching the documentary after the first twenty minutes, to be honest. I was just staring at the screen, and my body was like a statue. Because like I said, all the motion, all that exhaustion... it's entirely up in my head. The gears are constantly grinding up there, running through the safety protocols, double-checking the supply chain manifests in my mind, making sure I didn't overlook some tiny detail that's going to cause a structural failure or get one of my guys hurt. The mental checklist never, ever stops moving. But physically? No. I don't feel driven by a motor at all. 

If anything, when I have downtime, I want to move *less*. I just want to sit in that chair and try to process the heavy feeling in my gut. I don't wear out the carpets, I don't drive my wife crazy by hovering around the house. When I'm off the clock, I sit. So, pacing back and forth or needing to be in constant motion... no, I haven't experienced anything like that.
Have you ever thought that life wasn't worth living?

No, no, never. I've never thought that. Not for a single second. I mean, like I was saying before about knowing my worth and knowing I'm not a burden... that ties right into this. Life is absolutely worth living. I have way too much going on, way too many people counting on me to ever entertain a thought like that. 

I mean, sure, the mental exhaustion is real. I won't lie to you about that. Sitting in that recliner, feeling that heavy dread in my gut, just running through every single safety variable on the site—it's tiring. It really is. But it's tiring exactly because I care so much about *preserving* life, you know? My whole job, my whole mindset right now is about making sure things don't go wrong, making sure nobody gets hurt, making sure the structure holds up. If I didn't value life—my own or anyone else's—I wouldn't be agonizing over these details in the first place. 

And personally, outside of work, I have a great life. I really do. My wife and I, since we paid off that mortgage, we've actually been talking about buying a little property up near the lake. Nothing huge, maybe just a quarter acre with an older cabin that needs some structural rehab—which, obviously, is right up my alley. I've already been sketching out some ideas for how to reinforce a foundation on a slope like that, looking at grading and drainage solutions, because you have to be really careful with soil erosion near a body of water. You don't want to pour a concrete slab and have it crack right down the middle two winters later just because you didn't account for the freeze-thaw cycle and the hydrostatic pressure. I could spend weeks just mapping out the retaining walls. 

So, no. I have plans. I have things I want to build, things I want to do with my wife, guys on my crew who need me to sign off on their hours. The problem isn't that I don't want to live, or that I think life isn't worth it. The problem is just that I want to live without this... this constant alarm bell ringing in my head all the time. But giving up? Throwing in the towel? No, that's just not in my DNA. Never has been, never will be.
Do you think your family or loved ones would be better off without you?

No, absolutely not. I mean, I feel like we sort of covered this ground a little bit when you asked if I felt like a burden earlier, but... to be completely honest, I think everything would kind of fall apart without me. Not to sound arrogant, it's just the reality of how our family operates. 

My wife, for instance, she's an incredibly talented woman, she really is, but she's a big-picture thinker. She doesn't do the minutiae. If I weren't here, I don't know who would keep track of... well, everything. The property taxes, the insurance policies, the vehicles. I actually keep a meticulous spreadsheet for the maintenance on both our cars—tire rotations, oil changes, checking the brake pads, you name it. Just last week I spent two hours flushing the radiator on her SUV because the coolant was looking a little sludgy, and you really don't want to mess around with engine overheating, especially with the summer temperatures we've been getting lately. If that block cracks, you're looking at a total engine replacement, which is easily five or six grand. I handle all of that so she doesn't even have to think about it. 

And it's not just the cars or the house, it's the extended family, too. Like I was saying about my brother-in-law and the sump pump. If I wasn't around to go over there, he would have had thousands and thousands of dollars in water damage. He probably would have ended up with black mold creeping up the drywall, which is a massive health hazard, by the way. Once mold gets into the porous materials, you have to rip out the insulation, treat the framing, run commercial dehumidifiers for days... it's an absolute nightmare. I saved him from all of that because I know how to step in and manage a crisis. 

So, no. They definitely wouldn't be better off without me. I know this constant dread I'm dealing with is a lot, and it's exhausting for me to be running these mental safety checks all the time, but it doesn't make me a negative in their lives. I'm still the one keeping the ship steered straight, you know? They rely on me. I'm the anchor for a lot of people in my life, so... no, I've never once thought they'd be better off if I weren't here.
Have you ever had thoughts that you'd be better off dead?

No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I think that really just echoes what we were just talking about with the whole 'life not worth living' thing, or feeling like a burden. It's all in that same ballpark, right? And I'm just not in that ballpark. I've never had a thought like that, that I'd be better off dead. Not even a fleeting one. 

I know I talk a lot about this heavy feeling, this... this dread in my gut, and how the gears in my head are just constantly grinding, running through all the safety protocols and the what-ifs. And yeah, it wears me down. It's exhausting to always be on high alert, to always be the one looking out for the structural failures or the supply chain hiccups or the mold in the drywall. It takes a toll, I won't pretend it doesn't. Sometimes when I'm sitting in that recliner, I just wish I could find a switch to turn it off for an hour, just to get some peace and quiet in my own head. 

But wanting peace and quiet is a long, long way from wanting to be dead. Being dead doesn't solve anything. It just leaves a mess for everyone else to clean up. And like I said, I'm the guy who cleans up the messes. I'm the one who flushes the radiator and fixes the sump pump and plans out the retaining walls for the cabin we want to buy. I'm a project manager. I fix things. I build things. I don't just... walk off the job site forever. 

I mean, imagine the logistics of that, just from a practical standpoint. The absolute chaos it would cause for my wife, for my crew. Who's going to sign off on the safety inspections? Who's going to make sure the concrete cures properly before they start framing? You can't just leave those things to chance. It's irresponsible. And beyond the work stuff, I want to be here. I want to build that cabin. I want to figure out the drainage solutions for that sloped lot. I have things to do. So, no, I've never thought I'd be better off dead. I just want to figure out how to live without feeling like the sky is about to fall every single minute of the day. That's why I'm here talking to you.
Do you feel anxious most of the time?

Well, anxious... yeah, I suppose you could call it anxiety, but to me, it feels more like this... this constant, low-grade dread. And guilt, honestly. It's a heavy mix of dread and guilt that just follows me around, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. 

It's like this nagging feeling in the back of my head that I should have seen one more risk coming. In my line of work, we build these massive risk matrices, right? We calculate probability, we calculate impact, we assign mitigation strategies, and we put controls in place. And logically, I know we did all of that. People keep telling me—my colleagues, my boss, my wife—they all keep saying, "Look, the controls were in place. You followed the protocol to the letter." And I know they're right, at least on paper. But now? If I try to even think about going down to the shop, or heading down to the marina, or doing my shift at the society... it just feels like this massive weight. It all just feels like chores. Just another list of tasks I have to manage, another set of variables I have to monitor. I keep putting them off. Every weekend I tell my wife, 'Oh, I'll go down and calibrate the jointer this afternoon,' or 'I'll call the marina about the slip fees,' and then I just... don't. I sit in that recliner instead. Just to give you an example, on Tuesday, I had to sit down and review this massive, 400-page revision to an electrical plan because the city decided to update their compliance codes right in the middle of our Q3 timeline. I sat at my desk in the trailer, locked in, for maybe four and a half hours straight, just cross-referencing the new conduit requirements against our existing supply orders. Didn't miss a beat. I didn't find myself zoning out, I didn't have to re-read the same paragraph over and over to understand it. I actually caught three minor discrepancies that the engineering firm themselves missed.

The concentration is definitely there. It's just... the things my mind chooses to focus on when I'm *not* actively working on a task, you know? I mean, I can see why you might ask that, given the heavy guilt I was talking about earlier, feeling like I missed things or didn't do enough to foresee a risk. But there's a very big difference, at least in my mind, between feeling guilty about a specific protocol and feeling completely worthless as a person. 

I know my value. I've been in commercial project management for over twenty years now, and you just don't survive in this industry—managing multi-million dollar budgets, coordinating eighty different subcontractors on a tight footprint—if you're worthless. I know I'm good at what I do. I provide a very comfortable life for my wife. We actually managed to pay off our mortgage three years early, which is something I take a whole lot of pride in. 

And as for being a burden... no, if anything, I'm the one carrying the load for other people. I'm the guy everyone calls when things go sideways. Just to give you an idea, last weekend, my brother-in-law's sump pump failed in his basement. Who does he call at eleven o'clock on a Saturday night? Me. Because he knows I've got the heavy-duty wet-vac in the garage, I have the industrial fans, and I know exactly how to pull up the baseboards without completely ruining the drywall. I drove over there in the pouring rain and spent four hours bailing him out. Literally bailing him out. 

So, I'm definitely not a burden. People rely on me. My crew relies on me to keep the site safe and make sure the supply chains are moving so their paychecks clear, my wife relies on me, my extended family relies on me. Even with this dread hanging over me, this constant, exhausting mental loop of re-checking my decisions to make sure nobody gets hurt... I know I'm useful. I know I have a purpose. I'm a provider and a problem-solver, and that fundamental part of who I am hasn't changed one bit. I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or thinking the world would be better off without me, or anything dramatic like that. I just want to figure out how to shut off the internal noise. But my actual self-worth? No, that's completely intact.

Anyway, I sat down in that chair, turned on a documentary about the engineering of the Panama Canal—which is fascinating, by the way, the sheer scale of the earth-moving they had to do back then with such limited technology—and I just sat there. The mental checklist never, ever stops moving. But physically? No. I don't feel driven by a motor at all.

Well, anxious... yeah, I suppose you could call it anxiety, but to me, it feels more like this... this constant, low-grade dread. And guilt, honestly. It's a heavy mix of dread and guilt that just follows me around, no matter where I am or what I'm doing. 

It's like this nagging feeling in the back of my head that I should have seen one more risk coming. In my line of work, we build these massive risk matrices, right? We calculate probability, we calculate impact, we assign mitigation strategies, and we put controls in place. And logically, I know we did all of that. People keep telling me—my colleagues, my boss, my wife—they all keep saying, "Look, the controls were in place. You followed the protocol to the letter." And I know they're right, at least on paper. I can look at the documentation and see that the safety checks were signed off, the redundancies were active, the compliance audits were totally clear. 

But knowing that logically doesn't stop this feeling in my gut. It doesn't stop the guilt. Because when you're the project manager, the buck stops with you. If a supply chain fails, if a structural support is compromised, if a safety tolerance is off by a fraction of a millimeter... you're the guy who was supposed to catch it. So even when everyone is telling me I did everything right and the controls were exactly what they were supposed to be, I still wake up with that pit in my stomach. 

I'll be sitting in my recliner at night, trying to just watch a baseball game or something normal, and my brain is just running through the fault tree analysis over and over again. I'm thinking, what if I had just looked a little harder? What if I had run just one more scenario, or double-checked one more variable? Could I have anticipated it? So yeah, it's a kind of anxiety, but it's really rooted in this profound sense of responsibility that just never shuts off. It's just this shadow of dread that I missed something, and it's there from the minute I wake up to the minute I finally manage to fall asleep.

Sleep... yeah. Well, the first part of the night is actually fine. I'm a pretty disciplined guy, so I make sure I get to bed at a reasonable hour. But then... it's almost like clockwork. Right around two or three in the morning, my eyes just snap open. It’s not a slow, groggy wake-up, either. I’ll be lying there in the pitch black, and I’m visualizing the site layout, running through the load-bearing tolerances on the steel framing, or wondering if the soil compaction reports were properly verified before the foundation pour. The ice maker drops a batch of ice down in the kitchen, and my pulse just jumps until I can categorize the noise and verify exactly what it was. So I might be physically in the bed until my alarm goes off, but I'm certainly not getting any real rest. It's just hours of lying there, monitoring the house and re-running the job site variables until the sun finally comes up.
